title: Labor market impacts of AI: A new measure and early evidence
author: Maxim Massenkoff · Peter McCrory

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Aggregate productivity: Task speedups shrink during scaling
st.an: The excerpt describes empirical methods for measuring AI exposure, adoption and labour-market responses, but supplies no findings on aggregate productivity, verification, residual tasks, employment reallocation or welfare. It therefore does not establish support for or opposition to the cluster’s proposition.
qs: Johnston and Makridis (2025) do a similar task-based analysis using US administrative data, but they aggregate treatment to the industry level.

st.t: Assisted inequality: Productivity gains need not improve careers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s separation of AI exposure from realized labour-market outcomes. Its task-based framework identifies potentially affected workers, while its early post-ChatGPT comparison finds no statistically significant unemployment divergence and explicitly cautions that important effects may not yet be visible or fully captured.
qs: This approach won't capture every channel through which AI could reshape the labor market, but by laying this groundwork now, before meaningful effects have emerged, we hope future findings will more reliably identify economic disruption than post-hoc analyses.

st.t: Entry routes: Reduced hiring precedes broader displacement
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition: it finds no detected unemployment effect while identifying tentative, borderline-significant evidence of reduced hiring into AI-exposed occupations among workers aged 22–25. It also reinforces the cluster’s caution that weaker entry does not itself prove displacement or unemployment, because affected workers may remain employed, switch occupations or return to education.
qs: Using survey data from the US, we find no impact on unemployment rates for workers in the most exposed occupations, although there’s tentative evidence that hiring into those professions has slowed slightly for workers aged 22-25.
The averaged estimate in the post-ChatGPT era is a 14% drop in the job finding rate compared to that in 2022 in the exposed occupations, although this is just barely statistically significant.

It does not independently address unemployment or reduced junior hiring, so its support is methodological rather than direct evidence of those labour-market outcomes.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s cautious distinction between technical exposure and realised displacement. It finds no systematic unemployment increase among highly exposed workers, while identifying only tentative, barely significant evidence of slower entry into exposed occupations for workers aged 22–25. This aligns with concentrated entry-level pressure rather than demonstrated profession-wide job loss, though the study is economy-wide rather than specific to legal work.
qs: The averaged estimate in the post-ChatGPT era is a 14% drop in the job finding rate compared to that in 2022 in the exposed occupations, although this is just barely statistically significant.

st.t: Observed use: Capability predictions exceed workplace adoption
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central distinction between theoretical task capability and observed workplace use. Its occupational exposure measure combines feasibility with actual professional Claude usage, reports a large capability–adoption gap, and identifies verification, legal, software and model constraints as adoption barriers without treating exposure as evidence of job displacement.
qs: ### A new measure of occupational exposure  Our new measure, observed exposure*, is meant to quantify: of those tasks that LLMs could theoretically speed up, which are actually seeing automated usage in professional settings?
For instance, Claude currently covers just 33% of all tasks in the Computer & Math category.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s task-level, non-deterministic account of AI capability and labour effects. It distinguishes theoretical capability from observed use, finds substantial occupational and task variation, and reports no statistically distinguishable post-ChatGPT unemployment effect for highly exposed workers, while treating that result as early and subject to reassessment. It does not directly address legal workflow redesign, verification or user expertise.
qs: Our work follows this task-based approach, incorporating measures of theoretical AI capability and real-world usage, before aggregating to occupations.3  ## Measuring exposure  Our approach combines data from three sources.

kp.k: Observed exposure combines capability with actual workplace usage
kp.d: The authors introduce “observed exposure,” an occupation-level measure combining O*NET task data, Eloundou et al.’s theoretical LLM exposure estimates, and Claude usage from the Anthropic Economic Index. Tasks count as covered when theoretically feasible and sufficiently observed in work-related Claude traffic; automated implementations receive full weight, augmentative uses half weight, and task scores are weighted by time spent within each occupation.
qs: We introduce a new measure of AI displacement risk, observed exposure*, that combines theoretical LLM capability and real-world usage data, weighting automated (rather than augmentative) and work-related uses more heavily
We count tasks that are theoretically capable with an LLM as covered if they have seen sufficient work-related usage in Claude traffic.
We then adjust for how the task is being carried out: fully automated implementations receive full weight, while augmentative use receives half weight.
Finally, the task-level coverage measures are averaged to the occupation level weighted by the fraction of time spent on each task.

kp.k: Actual AI coverage remains far below theoretical capability
kp.d: Observed Claude usage is concentrated in tasks already classified as theoretically feasible, but workplace adoption covers only a fraction of the theoretically exposed task space. Across four prior Economic Index reports, 97% of observed tasks were theoretically feasible; 68% of usage involved tasks feasible for an LLM alone and 3% involved tasks rated infeasible. Claude covered 33% of Computer & Math tasks, compared with 94% theoretical exposure.
qs: As Figure 1 shows, 97% of the tasks observed across the previous four Economic Index reports fall into categories rated as theoretically feasible by Eloundou et al. (β=0.5 or β=1.0).
Tasks rated β=1 (fully feasible for an LLM alone) account for 68% of observed Claude usage, while tasks rated β=0 (not feasible) account for just 3%.
The coverage shows AI is far from reaching its theoretical capabilities.
For instance, Claude currently covers just 33% of all tasks in the Computer & Math category.

kp.k: Automation, adoption, and diffusion determine occupational exposure
kp.d: The measure treats theoretical capability as insufficient for displacement risk: exposure rises when feasible tasks are actually performed through work-related, automated, or API-based use and constitute a larger share of the occupation. The authors identify model limitations, legal constraints, software needs, and human verification as reasons actual use may lag capability.
qs: Our new measure, observed exposure*, is meant to quantify: of those tasks that LLMs could theoretically speed up, which are actually seeing automated usage in professional settings?
A job's exposure is higher if:
Its tasks are performed in work-related contexts
It has a relatively higher share of automated use patterns or API implementation
Others may be slow to diffuse due to legal constraints, specific software requirements, human verification steps, or other hurdles.

kp.k: Programming and customer service show highest observed exposure
kp.d: Computer Programmers rank first at 75% task coverage, followed by Customer Service Representatives, while Data Entry Keyers are 67% covered. Conversely, 30% of workers have zero measured coverage because their tasks appear too infrequently in the usage data, including many physical and in-person service occupations.
qs: Figure 3 shows the ten occupations most exposed under this measure.

In line with other data showing that Claude is extensively used for coding, Computer Programmers are at the top, with 75% coverage, followed by Customer Service Representatives, whose main tasks we increasingly see in first-party API traffic.
Finally, Data Entry Keyers, whose primary task of reading source documents and entering data sees significant automation, are 67% covered.
At the bottom end, 30% of workers have zero coverage, as their tasks appeared too infrequently in our data to meet the minimum threshold.

kp.k: Some legal tasks remain beyond current AI reach
kp.d: The report does not analyze the legal profession separately, but identifies legal constraints and verification as adoption barriers and representing clients in court as an example of work beyond AI’s present reach. This distinguishes theoretically or technically automatable tasks from legal work that still requires human performance.
qs: Others may be slow to diffuse due to legal constraints, specific software requirements, human verification steps, or other hurdles.

There is a large uncovered area too; many tasks, of course, remain beyond AI's reach—from physical agricultural work like pruning trees and operating farm machinery to legal tasks like representing clients in court.

kp.k: Higher exposure correlates with weaker projected job growth
kp.d: Using BLS projections published in 2025 for employment changes from 2024 to 2034, the authors find a slight negative association: each 10-percentage-point rise in observed coverage corresponds to a 0.6-percentage-point reduction in projected growth. They present this as limited validation against independent forecasts, not evidence of realized AI-caused job loss; theoretical exposure alone has no such correlation.
qs: For every 10 percentage point increase in coverage, the BLS’s growth projection drops by 0.6 percentage points.
This provides some validation in that our measures track the independently derived estimates from labor market analysts, although the relationship is slight.
Interestingly, there is no such correlation using the Eloundou et al. measure alone.

kp.k: Highly exposed workers differ sharply from unexposed workers
kp.d: Pre-ChatGPT Current Population Survey data from August through October 2022 show that workers in the highest exposure quartile were more likely to be female, white, Asian, highly educated, and higher-paid than workers in the zero-exposure group. They earned 47% more on average; graduate-degree prevalence was 17.4% versus 4.5%.
qs: The more exposed group is 16 percentage points more likely to be female, 11 percentage points more likely to be white, and almost twice as likely to be Asian.
They earn 47% more, on average, and have higher levels of education.
For example, people with graduate degrees are 4.5% of the unexposed group, but 17. 4% of the most exposed group, an almost fourfold difference.

kp.k: No systematic unemployment increase appears after ChatGPT
kp.d: A Current Population Survey comparison between workers in the top exposure quartile and workers with zero exposure finds largely similar post-pandemic unemployment trends. The post-ChatGPT difference-in-differences estimate is small, statistically insignificant, and indistinguishable from zero. Appendix checks varying the exposure cutoff, focusing on ages 22–25, and using unemployment-insurance claimant data also find no clear effect.
qs: We find no systematic increase in unemployment for highly exposed workers since late 2022, though we find suggestive evidence that hiring of younger workers has slowed in exposed occupations
Since then, the trends have been largely similar between the two groups.

The average change in the gap since the release of ChatGPT is small and insignificant, suggesting that the unemployment rate of the more exposed group has increased slightly but the effect is indistinguishable from zero.
In no extension do we find clear impacts on exposed jobs.

kp.k: The analysis could detect large differential unemployment shocks
kp.d: The authors estimate that the framework could detect a differential unemployment increase of roughly 1 percentage point. They illustrate that laying off all workers in the top 10% would raise unemployment within the top exposure quartile from 3% to 43% and aggregate unemployment from 4% to 13%; a white-collar analogue of the Great Recession would raise top-quartile unemployment from 3% to 6% and should also be visible.
qs: Based on the confidence interval of the pooled estimate, differential increases in unemployment on the order of 1 percentage point would be detectable (this will change as new data comes in, so it is merely a ballpark estimate).
If all workers within the top 10% were laid off, it would increase unemployment within the top quartile group from 3% to 43%, and it would increase aggregate unemployment from 4% to 13%.
Such a doubling in the top quartile of exposure would increase its unemployment rate from 3% to 6%.
This should be visible in our analysis as well.

kp.k: Young-worker hiring shows tentative exposure-related weakening
kp.d: For workers aged 22–25, unemployment in exposed occupations remains flat, but job starts diverge in 2024. Entry into the most exposed occupations declines by about half a percentage point while the unexposed rate remains at 2% per month. The post-ChatGPT estimate is a 14% reduction relative to 2022 and is only barely statistically significant; no comparable decrease appears for workers older than 25.
qs: We find that the unemployment rate for young workers in the exposed occupations is flat
Apart from some large swings in 2020-2021, these series visually diverge in 2024, with young workers relatively less likely to be hired into exposed occupations.
Job finding rates at the less exposed occupations remain stable at 2% per month, while entry into the most exposed jobs decreases by about half a percentage point.
The averaged estimate in the post-ChatGPT era is a 14% drop in the job finding rate compared to that in 2022 in the exposed occupations, although this is just barely statistically significant.
There is no such decrease for workers older than 25.

kp.k: Young hiring evidence has important alternative explanations
kp.d: The authors characterize the young-worker result as suggestive rather than causal. Workers not entering exposed occupations may remain in existing employment, choose different occupations, return to education, or leave the labor force; survey measurement error in job transitions is an additional concern.
qs: This may provide some signal of the early effects of AI on employment, and echoes the findings from Brynjolfsson et al.
But there are several alternative interpretations.
The young workers who are not hired may be remaining at their existing jobs, taking different jobs, or returning to school.
A further data-related caveat is that job transitions may be more vulnerable to mismeasurement in surveys.

kp.k: Unemployment is prioritized as the clearest harm measure
kp.d: The report prioritizes unemployment because it directly records unsuccessful job search and potential economic harm. Employment levels or postings may shift without comparable harm if workers move into related roles, while labor-force exits by new entrants mean that hiring slowdowns may not appear in occupation-coded unemployment data.
qs: We focus on unemployment as our priority outcome because it most directly captures the potential for economic harm—a worker who is unemployed wants a job and has not yet found one.

In this case, job postings and employment do not necessarily signal the need for policy responses; a decline in job postings for a highly exposed role may be counteracted by increased openings in a related one.
Most harmful labor market developments of AI should arguably include a period of increased unemployment, as displaced workers search for alternatives.

But slowed hiring may not necessarily manifest as increased unemployment, since many young workers are labor market entrants without a listed occupation in the CPS data and may exit the labor force rather than appear as unemployed.

kp.k: Task structure may delay or offset employment effects
kp.d: The report cites competing mechanisms for translating task exposure into labor demand. An O-ring model implies effects may appear only after AI penetrates every task; concentrated exposure in only some tasks may counteract the demand reduction associated with average exposure; and the expertise required for remaining human tasks may also shape outcomes. The authors therefore assume only that the most exposed workers should be affected first.
qs: Gans and Goldfarb (2025) show that if an O-ring model best describes jobs, employment effects might be seen only when all tasks have some degree of AI penetration.
Hampole et al. (2025) argue that mean exposure decreases labor demand, but concentration* of exposure in only certain tasks can counteract this.
And Autor and Thompson (2025) highlight the level of expertise required for the remaining tasks.
But we make the assumption that impacts should affect the most exposed workers first, and present results varying the cutoff we use to define treatment.

kp.k: Causal interpretation requires a credible counterfactual
kp.d: The authors caution that AI’s labor effects may be gradual and obscured by trade policy, economic cycles, and other forces, unlike the sudden COVID-19 shock. Their main design compares more- and less-exposed groups and identifies differential rather than economy-wide changes, so parallel unemployment increases across all workers would not be attributed to AI under this framework.
qs: The impacts of AI, however, might be less like COVID and more like the internet or trade with China.
The effects may not be immediately clear from aggregate unemployment data; factors like trade policy and the business cycle could cloud interpretations of trend lines.
One common approach is to compare outcomes between more or less AI-exposed workers, firms, or industries, in order to isolate the effect of AI from confounding forces.
If unemployment increased for all workers in parallel, we would not attribute this to AI advancements that still leave many tasks unaffected.

kp.k: Historical forecasting failures motivate analytical humility
kp.d: The report frames its evidence as preliminary because past measures and forecasts have often failed to predict labor-market disruption accurately. It notes that many jobs classified as offshorable subsequently grew, official occupational forecasts have added little beyond extrapolation, and studies of robots and the China trade shock remain disputed.
qs: But the track record of past approaches gives reason for humility.
For example, a prominent attempt to measure job offshorability identified roughly a quarter of US jobs as vulnerable, but a decade on, most of those jobs maintained healthy employment growth.
The government’s own occupational growth forecasts, while directionally correct, have added little predictive value beyond linear extrapolation of past trends.
Studies on the employment effects of industrial robots reach opposing conclusions, and the scale of job losses attributed to the China trade shock continues to be debated.

kp.k: Results are platform-specific and methodologically judgment-dependent
kp.d: Observed exposure derives from Claude traffic rather than economy-wide AI use and uses Anthropic Economic Index datasets covering August and November 2025. The construction requires judgments about feasibility scores, significant usage, rare tasks, semantic matching, and the relative weights for automation and augmentation, although the authors report very high rank correlations across alternative specifications.
qs: We use the previous two Anthropic Economic Index datasets, covering usage from August and November 2025.
There are judgment calls involved at every step.
How much more should automation workflows count compared to augmentation?
A reassuring finding which we expand on in the Appendix is that the Spearman (rank-rank) correlation of job exposure across many resolutions to these questions is exceedingly high.

kp.k: The framework is designed for repeated future measurement
kp.d: The authors present the report as groundwork rather than a final estimate of AI displacement. They plan to update usage data and extend the methodology to new settings; proposed improvements include refreshing the early-2023 theoretical exposure metric and studying how recent graduates with credentials in exposed fields navigate the labor market.
qs: Our goal is to establish an approach for measuring how AI is affecting employment, and to revisit these analyses periodically.
Our work is a first step toward cataloging the impact of AI on the labor market.
Our usage data will be incorporated in future updates, forming an evolving picture of task and job coverage in the economy.
The Eloundou et al. metric could also be updated, to the extent that it is linked to LLM capabilities as of early 2023.

And, given the suggestive results around young workers and labor market entrants, a key next step might be to look at how recent graduates with educational credentials in exposed areas are navigating the labor market.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Massenkoff and McCrory report limited evidence of US employment effects so far: no systematic increase in unemployment among highly AI-exposed workers, but tentative evidence of slower hiring of young workers.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain labor-market study, not a study of legal services. The authors find that the post-ChatGPT change in the unemployment gap between highly exposed and unexposed occupations is small and statistically indistinguishable from zero. Their hiring analysis finds a 14% decline in the job-finding rate into exposed occupations for workers aged 22–25 relative to 2022, barely statistically significant, with no corresponding decrease for workers older than 25. They interpret the hiring result as a possible early AI effect rather than established causal displacement.

pts.k: Actual professional AI usage covers substantially fewer tasks than theoretical capability permits; the authors expect that coverage to expand with capability, adoption and deployment.
pts.d: The authors introduce 'observed exposure' as a displacement-risk measure combining theoretical task speedup potential with observed work-related Claude usage, weighting automation more heavily than augmentation. They report 33% observed coverage in Computer & Math versus 94% theoretical exposure, 75% coverage for computer programmers and 67% for data entry keyers. Thirty percent of workers have zero measured coverage because their tasks do not meet the usage threshold; this does not establish that those tasks are impossible to automate. Their explicit legal example is representing clients in court, which they describe as beyond AI's reach. They offer no separate prediction about lawyer employment or law-firm markets.

pts.k: Higher observed AI exposure is associated with slightly weaker BLS employment-growth projections through 2034.
pts.d: Massenkoff and McCrory report that each 10-percentage-point increase in observed coverage corresponds to a 0.6-percentage-point reduction in projected occupational employment growth. They present this as modest validation against independently derived labor-market projections, not as a measured causal effect of AI or their own forecast of job losses. They find no comparable correlation using theoretical exposure alone.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The findings combine task-level capability estimates and proprietary Claude usage with US occupational projections and household-survey labor-market outcomes.
pts.d: Observed exposure combines O*NET tasks for approximately 800 occupations, Eloundou et al. (2023) estimates of whether LLMs can at least double task speed, and Anthropic Economic Index usage. The exposure construction uses August and November 2025 usage datasets; the separate capability–usage comparison draws on four previous Economic Index reports. Automated implementations receive full weight and augmentation half weight, with occupation-level aggregation weighted by time spent on tasks. Employment-growth associations use an employment-weighted regression on BLS 2024–2034 projections. Unemployment and hiring estimates use the Current Population Survey (CPS), comparing high- and zero-exposure groups in a difference-in-differences framework; hiring uses respondents' month-to-month job transitions. The authors also report no clear unemployment effects in appendix checks varying exposure cutoffs, examining young workers and using unemployment-insurance claimant data. Brynjolfsson et al.'s cited employment declines are external findings, not this paper's own estimates.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The report assesses early post-ChatGPT outcomes, with hiring divergence visible in 2024; its longer-run coverage prediction has no fixed deadline.
pts.d: Published March 5, 2026 and corrected March 8 to fix reversed Figure 7 group labels, the report examines unemployment trends from 2016 and post-release changes since late 2022. The supplied text does not specify the final CPS observation month. Its exposure data reflect 2025 Claude usage, while theoretical capability estimates are linked to early 2023 models. The BLS projection horizon is 2024–2034. Future expansion of coverage is conditional on capabilities, adoption and deployment, with legal constraints, software requirements and human verification identified as diffusion hurdles. The unemployment design assumes the most exposed workers should be affected first and measures differential changes rather than economy-wide parallel increases. The authors estimate that roughly a one-percentage-point differential unemployment increase would be detectable. They caution that young entrants can be missed by occupation-based unemployment measures, and that slower observed hiring could reflect staying in existing jobs, taking other jobs, returning to school or survey mismeasurement. Illustrative mass-layoff and white-collar recession scenarios describe the framework's detection capacity, not predictions.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Exposure is concentrated in certain knowledge-work and administrative occupations, with a possible hiring disadvantage for workers aged 22–25 rather than demonstrated widespread unemployment.
pts.d: The authors identify computer programmers, customer service representatives and financial analysts among the most exposed occupations, and substantial automation coverage for data entry keyers. Relative to workers with zero measured exposure, those in the top exposure quartile are described as older, more often female, more educated and higher-paid. CPS characteristics measured in August–October 2022 show the exposed group is 16 percentage points more likely to be female, 11 points more likely to be white, almost twice as likely to be Asian and earns 47% more on average; graduate-degree holders constitute 17.4% versus 4.5%. These are exposure-group characteristics, not evidence that those demographic groups have lost jobs. Low-coverage examples include cooks, motorcycle mechanics, lifeguards, bartenders and dishwashers. Recent graduates and labor-market entrants are highlighted for further study. No legal occupation-specific employment effects are estimated.
